v.why: Very strong L2 penalty causes underfitting, so reducing alpha recovers large accuracy gains.
Increasing an already huge L2 penalty pushes weights toward zero and worsens underfitting.
Adam with very large learning rates diverges or collapses, and going higher worsens it.
Lowering an excessively large learning rate restores stable training.
Tiny learning rates undertrain in 243 epochs, so increasing them helps.
Deeper networks are less stable at high learning rates and often fail to train.
Shallower networks tolerate large learning rates better, so removing a layer helps.

raw:
These ten hypotheses come from the 100 single-seed measurements plus general knowledge of how ReLU MLPs behave with Adam. I did not run any new experiments. The strongest evidence is for the learning-rate and alpha interactions; the batch-size ones rest on weaker, noisier patterns.

- **Alpha, high band (alpha ≥ 0.129):** Heavy L2 penalties underfit badly. Rows 11, 12, 18 and 19 show large gains from stepping alpha down, and row 9 shows a loss from stepping it up.
- **Learning rate, high band (≥ 0.0774):** Adam diverges or collapses at these rates. Stepping up hurts a lot (rows 47–49), and stepping down helps (rows 51–54). Adding depth or width at high rates also hurts a lot (rows 62, 66, 68, 90), and removing depth helps (rows 72, 77).
- **Learning rate, low band:** At rates this small the model is undertrained, so stepping up helps (rows 41–43).
- **Batch size, low band:** Rows 21–24 show tiny batches are noisy and slow, and stepping up tends to help. In the high band, stepping down tends to hurt (rows 31, 32).
